elements.quote: Background: The aim of this systematic review is to examine the epidemiological knowledge and gaps in understanding of the potential causes of chronic kidney disease of undetermined cause (CKDu) in Meso-America.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: The aim of this systematic review is to examine the epidemiological knowledge and gaps in understanding of the potential causes of chronic kidney disease of undetermined cause (CKDu) in Meso-America.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit statement of the main objective/review question.
The abstract does not specify the main inclusion and exclusion criteria (only the Methods list databases and dates). Inclusion/exclusion details appear elsewhere but are not reported in the abstract.

elements.quote: Methods: A systematic literature search of epidemiological studies of CKDu was conducted in PubMed, Embase and Web of Science from January 2000 to January 2017.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the information sources used and the date range / last search date.

elements.quote: Study quality was assessed by adapting the tool from Higgins et al. for observational studies.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used to assess study quality/risk of bias (adapted Higgins et al. tool).

elements.quote: Where applicable, the summary prevalence odds ratio (POR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated using a random effects model.
elements.reason: The abstract states the synthesis method (calculation of summary PORs with 95% CI using a random effects model).

elements.quote: Results: Twenty-five epidemiological studies were included in the analysis of risk factors for CKDu.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (25) but does not report the total number of participants and provides only minimal study characteristic summary (quality described as medium), so the element is only partially satisfied.

elements.quote: The PORs for CKDu were males versus females 2.42 (95% CI 1.76-3.08), family history of CKD (versus none) 1.84 (95% CI 1.37-2.30), high water intake (versus low) 1.61 (95% CI 1.01-2.21) and low altitude (versus highland) 2.09 (95% CI 1.00-3.17).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes including effect estimates and CIs, but does not report the number of included studies or participants contributing to each outcome, so it partially meets the requirement.

elements.quote: Where applicable, the summary prevalence odds ratio (POR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated using a random effects model. The PORs for CKDu were males versus females 2.42 (95% CI 1.76-3.08) ...
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports summary estimates with 95% confidence intervals for main comparisons.

elements.quote: The PORs for CKDu were males versus females 2.42 (95% CI 1.76-3.08) ... Conclusion: Our meta-analysis showed positive associations for males (versus females) and family history of CKD, water intake, lowland altitude and CKDu.
elements.reason: When groups are compared the abstract indicates the direction of effect (e.g. males have higher odds than females) and which group is associated with higher risk.

The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision). Limitations are discussed elsewhere in the paper but are not reported in the abstract.

elements.quote: Conclusion: Our meta-analysis showed positive associations for males (versus females) and family history of CKD, water intake, lowland altitude and CKDu. There were no significant associations with pesticide exposure, non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs intake, heat stress and alcohol consumption.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and summarizes key implications regarding which factors showed associations.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding. Although a Funding section exists in the paper, funding is not reported in the abstract.
The abstract does not provide a registry name or registration number for the review.

elements.quote: Meso-American nephropathy (MeN), also known as chronic kidney disease of undetermined aetiology (CKDu), is a growing public health problem and young agricultural workers of the Pacific coast of Meso-America have been the most affected group [1-3]. There was an increased recognition of this problem by researchers, universities and policymakers after 2000 due to a marked increase in mortality and morbidity [4]. ... In the last 10 years, several narrative reviews about CKDu have been published [6-9]. None of these have conducted a formal meta-analysis and there was no systematic assessment of the quality of the available evidence considering inherent limitations within the design and analyses of available epidemiological studies.
elements.reason: Introduction describes the current state of knowledge (growing public health problem, groups affected, prior narrative reviews) and highlights important uncertainties (no formal meta-analysis and lack of systematic quality assessment).

elements.quote: The purpose of this study is therefore to formally examine the epidemiological knowledge and gaps in understanding of the potential causes of CKD of undetermined cause in Meso-America.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the aim and justifies the need to formally examine epidemiological knowledge and gaps, explaining why the review is important.

elements.quote: In the last 10 years, several narrative reviews about CKDu have been published [6-9]. None of these have conducted a formal meta-analysis and there was no systematic assessment of the quality of the available evidence considering inherent limitations within the design and analyses of available epidemiological studies.
elements.reason: The authors note existing narrative reviews and explicitly explain the need for the current systematic review and meta-analysis because prior reviews lacked formal meta-analysis and systematic quality assessment.
This review concerns epidemiological risk factors for CKDu rather than effects of interventions; no intervention mechanism is relevant to the manuscript.
The review does not address complex interventions or delivery contexts and does not present or require a logic model.

elements.quote: The search was limited to 'adolescent and adult human beings' and only papers published in English and Spanish languages were considered. The search was restricted to studies conducted in Meso-America (Central America and Mexico). The exposures of interest included heat stress, dehydration, pesticide, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), workplace conditions, environmental toxins and infectious diseases. The outcomes of interest included the reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), elevated serum creatinine (SCr) and CKD of undetermined cause. A wide range of study designs were assessed, including cross-sectional studies, case-control studies, retrospective or prospective cohort studies and ecological studies. We excluded animal studies, editorials, systematic reviews and case reports (Supplementary data, Table S4).
elements.reason: Study eligibility characteristics are specified: population age group, geographic setting, exposures and outcomes of interest, and eligible study designs; exclusions (animal studies, editorials, systematic reviews, case reports) are stated.

elements.quote: We searched on PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase and Web Science to identify all original research that had been published between January 2005 and January 2017 reporting prevalence and mortality of CKDu in Meso-America.
elements.reason: The time period for eligible reports is specified (January 2005 to January 2017); language restriction is specified elsewhere (text_5: English and Spanish), satisfying report-characteristic eligibility requirements.

elements.quote: 37 Full-text articles excluded: ... 2 Occupational studies without CKDu outcome
elements.reason: The flow diagram and text explicitly list exclusions for studies lacking the CKDu outcome (i.e. outcome not measured), but there is no explicit discussion distinguishing those exclusions from instances where outcomes were measured but outcome results were not reported; therefore the distinction is only partially addressed.

elements.quote: Where there were several studies with similar exposure definitions, data were included in a random effects meta-analysis for the respective exposure and CKDu and displayed in a forest plot.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies how studies were grouped for syntheses (by similar exposure definitions) and that these groupings were used in random-effects meta-analyses; text_9 further lists the specific risk-factor groups used (male sex, family history, water intake, pesticide exposure, alcohol, NSAIDs, heat stress, altitude).

elements.quote: The search was limited to 'adolescent and adult human beings' and only papers published in English and Spanish languages were considered. The search was restricted to studies conducted in Meso-America (Central America and Mexico).
elements.reason: Notable restrictions on study eligibility (age range, language, geographic restriction) are stated, but no rationale explaining why these restrictions were applied is provided in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: The full search strategy is outlined in the Supplementary Material (Supplementary data, Tables S1-S3).
elements.reason: The manuscript states that the full search strategy is provided in the Supplementary Material, but the complete search strings as actually run for each database are not present in the provided main-text evidence. The available evidence indicates the strategies exist externally but does not itself report the complete strategies.

elements.quote: We searched on PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase and Web Science to identify all original research that had been published between January 2005 and January 2017... The search was limited to 'adolescent and adult human beings' and only papers published in English and Spanish languages were considered. The search was restricted to studies conducted in Meso-America (Central America and Mexico).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports temporal limits (January 2005 to January 2017), population limits (adolescent and adult humans), language limits (English and Spanish), and geographic restriction (Meso-America), which are search limits tied to the eligibility criteria.
No citation or description of published search approaches or filters, nor any description of adaptations of such filters, is present in the retrieved evidence.
No mention of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to identify or refine search terms is present in the provided evidence.
No information about tools used to translate search strings between sources is reported in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence contains no description of any validation of the search strategy or validation studies/processes.
There is no description or evidence of any peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) in the provided material.
The manuscript does not report that the search structure was not based on PICO nor describe a final conceptual structure or explorations used to develop the search.

elements.quote: All titles and abstracts were examined by one reviewer (M.G.-Q.) according to the above inclusion criteria. ... After review of the titles and abstract were independently reviewed by two authors (M.G.-Q. and D.N.). All full-text articles were assessed independently using the same criteria and included if both reviewers recommended inclusion. A second reviewer (D.N.) checked a sample of 45 titles and abstracts selected randomly after duplicated articles were removed.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the number of reviewers at each stage: one reviewer screened all titles/abstracts initially, two reviewers independently reviewed titles/abstracts and full texts, and a second reviewer checked a random sample of 45 titles/abstracts.

elements.quote: After review of the titles and abstract were independently reviewed by two authors (M.G.-Q. and D.N.). All full-text articles were assessed independently using the same criteria and included if both reviewers recommended inclusion.
elements.reason: The text explicitly states that titles/abstracts and all full-text articles were reviewed independently by two authors.

elements.quote: Any disagreement of some marginal cases were discussed between M.G.-Q., B.C. and D.N.
elements.reason: The authors describe resolving disagreements by discussion among the named reviewers (M.G.-Q., B.C. and D.N.).
No text describes contacting study investigators or processes used to obtain or confirm eligibility information from investigators.
No methods for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment (e.g., translation procedures or languages handled) are reported.
There is no mention of automation tools (e.g., software, machine assistance) being integrated into the selection process.
The manuscript does not identify any externally derived classifiers, their versions/references, roles, or records removed before screening attributable to such classifiers.
No internally derived classifiers, nor descriptions of their use, training, or validation, are reported.
There is no description of machine-learning prioritisation tools or stopping/prioritisation rules used in screening.
No use of crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection is reported.

elements.quote: Title duplicates n=56
elements.reason: While the flow diagram (text_9 figure_5) shows duplicate records removed, the manuscript does not describe use of previously screened external datasets to eliminate records or how such datasets were derived; therefore the specific reporting item is not met.

elements.quote: The outcomes of interest included the reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), elevated serum creatinine (SCr) and CKD of undetermined cause.
elements.reason: The review explicitly lists and defines the outcome domains sought (reduced eGFR, elevated SCr, and CKD of undetermined cause).

elements.quote: Outcome definition | eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m 2 , by a second measurement of SCr within 3 months' difference
elements.reason: The review (in Table 2) specifies a time frame for the outcome definition for some studies (e.g. eGFR <60 defined by a second SCr measurement within 3 months), but does not consistently specify the measurement time frame for every outcome domain across all included studies.
No statement was found saying whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (e.g. all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.

The authors do not describe a process for selecting among multiple compatible results within outcome domains when not all results were sought; no selection methods for choosing among multiple measures/time-points within studies are reported.
No reporting of changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance with rationales was found in the provided evidence.
No reporting of changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains (or rationales for changes) was found.

elements.quote: Sufficient data for meta-analysis were available for a subset of risk factors: male sex, family history of CKD, water intake, pesticide exposure, alcohol consumption, self-medication with NSAIDs, heat stress and altitude.
elements.reason: The authors identify which outcomes/risk factors were used in meta-analyses (those considered for interpreting conclusions) and state this was driven by data availability, but they do not explicitly state that these were the 'most important' outcomes nor provide a detailed rationale beyond data sufficiency.

elements.quote: A standardized data extraction form was used by M.G.-Q. to extract study characteristics: authors, study design, year, country, sample size, altitude, exposure and outcome definitions, main findings, strengths and limitations and confounding factors.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists a set of other variables sought (authors, study design, year, country, sample size, altitude, exposure and outcome definitions, main findings, strengths and limitations, confounding factors) and states these were extracted using a standardized form.

No explicit description of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information is provided in the retrieved evidence. The text notes that difficulties were discussed jointly but does not state any assumptions applied to missing/unclear data.

elements.quote: A standardized data extraction form was used by M.G.-Q. to extract study characteristics: ...
elements.reason: The authors report using a standardized data extraction form (a tool) to determine and collect data items, but no citation or reference for this tool or form is provided in the retrieved evidence (whereas quality assessment tools are cited separately).

elements.quote: Quality was assessed for each selected study using standard quality assessment tools for trials [10] that we adapted for observational studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript cites using standard quality assessment tools (referring to Higgins et al. [10]) and states these were adapted for observational studies, but it does not specify the exact tool name/version or give full bibliographic or version details.

elements.quote: Studies were assigned a high, low or uncertain risk according to the following criteria: selection bias, non-differential measurement error for exposure and outcome, information bias in exposure and outcome, confounding and reverse causation.
elements.reason: The specific domains/components assessed by the risk-of-bias approach are listed explicitly (selection bias; measurement error for exposure and outcome; information bias in exposure and outcome; confounding; reverse causation).

elements.quote: Studies were assigned a high, low or uncertain risk according to the following criteria: selection bias, non-differential measurement error for exposure and outcome, information bias in exposure and outcome, confounding and reverse causation.
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgement (high/low/uncertain) was stated, but the manuscript does not report explicit rules or algorithms used to derive the overall judgement from the domain-level assessments.

elements.quote: Quality was assessed for each selected study using standard quality assessment tools for trials [10] that we adapted for observational studies.
elements.reason: The authors state they adapted a trials tool for observational studies (i.e. an adaptation was made) but they provide no details on what adaptations were made or how the tool was modified.
No evidence was found that the authors developed a new risk-of-bias tool; they report adapting an existing tool, so a newly developed tool does not apply.

elements.quote: All titles and abstracts were examined by one reviewer (M.G.-Q.) according to the above inclusion criteria. Any disagreement of some marginal cases were discussed between M.G.-Q., B.C. and D.N. After review of the titles and abstract were independently reviewed by two authors (M.G.-Q. and D.N.). All full-text articles were assessed independently using the same criteria and included if both reviewers recommended inclusion. A second reviewer (D.N.) checked a sample of 45 titles and abstracts selected randomly after duplicated articles were removed. Agreement between authors was quantified by j -statistic calculation.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes how study selection was performed and gives names/roles of reviewers and that assessments were independent for screening and full-text inclusion; however, it does not clearly state how many reviewers specifically performed the risk-of-bias / quality assessment, whether those assessments were independent, nor the exact procedures for resolving disagreements about risk-of-bias judgments.
No information is provided about contacting study investigators or processes used to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from original study authors.
There is no mention of any automation tools used for risk-of-bias assessment (use, training, performance, validation) in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Where applicable, the summary prevalence odds ratio (POR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated using a random effects model.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly specifies the effect measure used in synthesis/presentation (prevalence odds ratio, POR) and reports 95% CIs and use of a random-effects model.
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect size (e.g. what constitutes small/medium/large effects) or rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence.
There is no description in the supplied evidence of methods used to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure.
The provided text does not justify the choice of effect measure (no explicit rationale given for using POR or alternatives).

elements.quote: We reviewed the exposure and outcome definitions and reported risk factors in each study. Where there were several studies with similar exposure definitions, data were included in a random effects meta-analysis for the respective exposure and CKDu and displayed in a forest plot.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that the authors reviewed exposure and outcome definitions and that studies with similar exposure definitions were pooled for a random-effects meta-analysis for each exposure–CKDu pair, describing the process used to decide study eligibility for each synthesis.

elements.quote: We reviewed the exposure and outcome definitions and reported risk factors in each study. Where there were several studies with similar exposure definitions, data were included in a random effects meta-analysis for the respective exposure and CKDu and displayed in a forest plot. Funnel plot analysis and Egger's test were performed to detect publication bias and P < 0.05 was considered significant. The across-study heterogeneity was estimated by using Cochran's Q -statistic and calculating the proportion of total variability explained by heterogeneity ( I 2 ) described by Higgins et al . [10]. All analyses were performed using Stata version 14 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA).
elements.reason: The manuscript describes some data-preparation and synthesis procedures (reviewing exposure/outcome definitions, grouping similar exposures for random-effects meta-analysis, forest plots, tests for publication bias, heterogeneity measures, and software used). However, it does not report specific methods for preparing summary data such as handling missing summary statistics, data conversions, imputations, or other transformations—so the reporting is incomplete.

elements.quote: Table 1. Characteristics of occupational studies included in the systematic review ( n ¼ 5)
elements.reason: Tables (Table 1, Table 2) presenting study characteristics and outcome/exposure information are present and labelled (see Table 1 caption), but the Methods do not explicitly describe the tabular structures and which specific data fields would be included in each table (only the resulting tables appear in Results).

elements.quote: Where there were several studies with similar exposure definitions, data were included in a random effects meta-analysis for the respective exposure and CKDu and displayed in a forest plot. Funnel plot analysis and Egger's test were performed to detect publication bias and P < 0.05 was considered significant.
elements.reason: The Methods explicitly state the graphical methods used (forest plots for meta-analyses, funnel plots for publication bias) and related tests (Egger's).

elements.quote: Fig. 2. Forest plot of all prevalence of chronic kidney disease of undetermined cause (eGFR < 60mL/min/1.73 m 2 ) by age group and sex from 14 cross-sectional community studies identified.
elements.reason: The basis for grouping in at least one graph is reported: the forest plot is organised by age group and sex, as stated in the figure caption and described in Results.

No non-standard graphs are reported or described in the Methods or Results; only standard forest and funnel plots and a PRISMA flow diagram are mentioned, so a rationale for non-standard graphs does not apply.

The Methods / Data Synthesis text reports use of random-effects meta-analysis and measures of heterogeneity (Cochran's Q, I2) but does not specify any methods used to explore causes of heterogeneity such as subgroup analysis or meta-regression. (See text_8 which only describes meta-analysis, funnel plots, Egger's test, Cochran's Q and I2.)

No methods description was found reporting factors, factor levels, or the expected direction of effect modification for subgroup analyses or meta-regressions. The available text describes pooled analyses of specific exposures but does not pre-specify subgroup/meta-regression factors or effect directions.

The manuscript does not report whether heterogeneity analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both. The Methods describe random-effects meta-analysis and heterogeneity statistics (text_8) but do not state the level of covariates used for exploring heterogeneity.

No methods for comparing subgroup effects (e.g. tests for interaction or formal comparison procedures) are described in the Methods. The Results present pooled estimates for different exposures but do not report methods used to compare subgroup effects.

When meta-analysis was unsuitable the paper does not describe informal methods used to explore heterogeneity (e.g. narrative exploration specifying factors and levels). The text discusses study limitations and heterogeneity qualitatively but provides no specified informal heterogeneity-exploration methods.

There is no identification in the Methods or Results of analyses of heterogeneity that were not pre-specified. The paper does not state which heterogeneity analyses, if any, were post hoc versus pre-specified.

No text in the provided evidence describes any sensitivity analyses or details of sensitivity analyses performed. Methods mention random-effects meta-analysis, funnel plots, Egger's test, and heterogeneity measures (text_8), but do not report conducting or detailing sensitivity analyses.
There is no information in the supplied evidence identifying any sensitivity analyses, pre-specified or post-hoc. Therefore, no sensitivity analyses are reported or identified as not pre-specified.

elements.quote: Funnel plot analysis and Egger's test were performed to detect publication bias and P < 0.05 was considered significant.
elements.reason: The methods section explicitly states the use of funnel plots and Egger's test to detect publication bias (missing results arising from reporting biases).

elements.quote: Quality was assessed for each selected study using standard quality assessment tools for trials [10] that we adapted for observational studies. Studies were assigned a high, low or uncertain risk according to the following criteria: selection bias, non-differential measurement error for exposure and outcome, information bias in exposure and outcome, confounding and reverse causation.
elements.reason: An existing assessment approach was used and the assessed domains (selection bias, measurement error, information bias, confounding, reverse causation) and the overall judgment categories (high, low or uncertain risk) are reported.

elements.quote: Quality was assessed for each selected study using standard quality assessment tools for trials [10] that we adapted for observational studies.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state that they adapted a standard trials quality-assessment tool for observational studies, indicating an adaptation of an existing reporting-bias/quality tool.
No evidence that a newly developed reporting-bias tool was created or described; no description or public accessibility information is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: All titles and abstracts were examined by one reviewer (M.G.-Q.) according to the above inclusion criteria. Any disagreement of some marginal cases were discussed between M.G.-Q., B.C. and D.N. After review of the titles and abstract were independently reviewed by two authors (M.G.-Q. and D.N.). All full-text articles were assessed independently using the same criteria and included if both reviewers recommended inclusion. A second reviewer (D.N.) checked a sample of 45 titles and abstracts selected randomly after duplicated articles were removed. Agreement between authors was quantified by j -statistic calculation.
elements.reason: The number of reviewers (one initial, with checks and independent review by two authors), their independence (independent full-text assessment by two reviewers), and disagreement-resolution (discussion among named authors and quantification of agreement by j-statistic) are reported.
No information is provided in the retrieved evidence about processes used to obtain or confirm relevant information from study investigators.
No description of automation tools used for reporting-bias assessment (use, training, performance, validation) is present in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Quality was assessed for each selected study using standard quality assessment tools for trials [10] that we adapted for observational studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the source of the tool (standard quality assessment tools for trials, referencing Higgins et al.) and that it was adapted for observational studies, thereby specifying the tool/system used to assess study quality/certainty.

elements.quote: Studies were assigned a high, low or uncertain risk according to the following criteria: selection bias, non-differential measurement error for exposure and outcome, information bias in exposure and outcome, confounding and reverse causation.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists the specific factors considered in the assessment (selection bias, measurement error, information bias, confounding, reverse causation) and the criteria for assignment (high, low or uncertain risk).
No description or quote in the provided evidence specifies decision rules for deriving an overall certainty level for an outcome or interpretation of each level.

elements.quote: Epidemiological studies have underlined many potential risk factors for CKDu, including male sex, occupation, high ambient temperature, self-medication with NSAIDs, altitude, exposure to heavy metals or pesticides and genetic susceptibility [11, 1315, 18, 28]. While our systematic review could confirm the association with male sex, none of the other suggested risk factors were sufficiently well studied to conclusively prove or disprove their role. The most commonly cited working hypothesis for this disease has been heat stress causing repetitive episodes of dehydration in agricultural and non-agricultural workers due to working under heat stress and high humidity [15, 37], which may result in acute kidney injury (AKI) secondary to hypoperfusion or rhabdomyolysis [38]. However, although this hypothesis has been explored in an experimental study that suggested that dehydration and hyperosmolarity may induce tubular injury via activation of the polyolfructokinase pathway in the kidney [39], there have been no corresponding data in humans to support this hypothesis. ... Most of the studies that suggest a possible association between AKI and exposure to organochlorides, paraquat, 2,4-diclorophenoxyacetic and glyphosate have been conducted in animals [43, 44]. A single prospective cohort study among male licensed pesticide applicators in the USA reported an association between end-stage renal disease and exposure-response and increasing accumulated lifetime days in pesticide exposure and non-exposure for some herbicides such as alachlor, paraquat, pendimethalin, atrazine, permethrin and metolochlor [45].
